title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Addiction — October 2026

studies.title: Heavy phone use and depression travel together, but one may not be driving the other
studies.ns_score_reason: a rare four-wave, within-person test of the phone-causes-depression story that largely dissolves it; limited by self-report and a student sample.
studies.the_study: Chinese college students (N=851 retained) were surveyed four times across nine months, from September 2025 to June 2026, on problematic smartphone use (PSU) and depressive symptoms. Using random-intercept cross-lagged panel models, the researchers found that roughly half of the variance in PSU and around 60% of the variance in depressive symptoms was stable between-person difference — some people simply sit high on both. The within-person forward path from PSU to later depressive symptoms was small (β ≈ 0.13), the reverse path was not significant, the difference between directions was not statistically reliable, and the effect vanished altogether under an alternative model (LCM-SR).
studies.why_it_matters: Most of the correlation between problematic phone use and low mood appears to be a trait-like co-occurrence rather than a month-to-month process in which phone use pushes mood down — which weakens one of the most widely repeated claims in popular psychology.
studies.pitch_angle: Everyone "knows" the phone is making them sad. Open on a student who deletes an app every January — then show what happens when you track the same people four times and model within-person change instead of between-person snapshots: the effect shrinks to near nothing and flips depending on which model you run. Worth calling the corresponding authors Xinguo Zheng (Northwest Normal University) and Qi Hui (Xi'an University of Science and Technology), and an independent methodologist on why RI-CLPM keeps deflating screen-time findings.
studies.wider_angle: A methods-reckoning feature for a science or policy outlet on how the shift from cross-lagged to random-intercept models has quietly demolished a decade of "X predicts Y" findings across psychology — screens, social media, loneliness, sleep — and what that means for school phone bans already written into law.
studies.caveats: Observational design (cannot establish causation); all outcomes self-reported; single population of Chinese college students, may not generalize; 189 participants first observed at wave 2; findings explicitly model-dependent by the authors' own account.

studies.title: Seeing drug-related images breaks down basic sensory filtering in people who use methamphetamine
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean human brain-imaging result showing drug cues intrude on a process that isn't supposed to be cognitive at all; modest sample.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Seventy-two adults (35 who regularly use methamphetamine) underwent magnetoencephalography during a paired-pulse somatosensory gating task — a basic test of whether the brain suppresses its response to a repeated touch. Before each trial, participants glimpsed either a substance-related or a neutral image. The methamphetamine group showed weaker gating overall, and crucially only they gated worse after a drug image; they also had elevated spontaneous gamma activity in somatosensory cortex, consistent with disrupted GABAergic inhibition.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests cue reactivity in addiction isn't confined to reward circuitry and craving — a drug cue can degrade low-level sensory filtering within a fraction of a second, which may help explain why environments saturated with reminders are so destabilizing.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the surprise: a picture of a pipe makes the brain worse at ignoring a repeated touch on the hand. Open with the paradox of relapse triggered by walking down a familiar street, then explain what sensory gating is and why its collapse implies drug cues hijack the brain far earlier in processing than craving models assume. Tony W. Wilson's group at the Institute for Human Neuroscience, Boys Town National Research Hospital, is the call.
studies.wider_angle: For a health or neurology outlet: sensory gating as an underused clinical readout. The same paired-pulse measure is abnormal in schizophrenia and PTSD — a piece on whether a cheap, passive index of cortical inhibition could become a cross-diagnostic biomarker, and what GABAergic damage from stimulants means for long-term cognition.
studies.caveats: Small N (72, with 35 in the exposure group); cross-sectional and observational — cannot show whether gating deficits precede or follow methamphetamine use; single center; polysubstance use and abstinence duration not detailed in the abstract.

studies.title: What gamblers believe about gambling predicts their trajectory better than how well they manage emotions
studies.ns_score_reason: a longitudinal head-to-head that demotes the fashionable emotion-regulation explanation; only two waves.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Five hundred eighty-five Chinese adult lifetime gamblers (mean age 30, 48% women) completed online questionnaires at two time points. In a cross-lagged panel model, metacognitions about gambling — beliefs such as "gambling helps me control my thoughts" or "my urge to gamble is uncontrollable" — were stronger prospective predictors of gambling disorder tendency than emotion regulation ability was. Negative metacognitions were themselves predicted by earlier gambling disorder severity, indicating a self-feeding loop, with emotion regulation appearing to buffer it.
studies.why_it_matters: If beliefs about one's own thinking, rather than raw emotional coping, drive the escalation of gambling problems, treatment should target those beliefs directly — which is what metacognitive therapy does, and which differs from standard cognitive behavioral approaches focused on gambling fallacies.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is that the problem isn't that gamblers can't handle their feelings — it's what they believe about their own urges, and the belief that an urge is uncontrollable helps make it so. Open on the vicious circle: losing more makes you believe you can't stop, which makes you less able to stop. Call Marcantonio M. Spada (London South Bank University) on metacognitive therapy, and Anise M. S. Wu (University of Macau) on gambling in Macau.
studies.wider_angle: For a features desk: the quiet spread of metacognitive therapy out of anxiety and depression into addiction, gaming and smartphone use — treating the belief about the thought rather than the thought. Pair with the awkward politics of gambling research funding.
studies.caveats: Observational, two waves only (limits causal inference); all self-reported; online convenience sample of Chinese gamblers, may not generalize; funders include Chongqing municipal social science and education commission programs.

studies.title: Self-control protects teenagers from internet addiction — except when they are being punished
studies.ns_score_reason: large sample and a genuinely odd non-linear reversal; cross-sectional and the reversal needs replicating.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A survey of 4,305 Chinese high school students broke self-control into self-regulation and impulse inhibition, and negative life events into separate domains, then combined mediation and network analysis. Lower self-control predicted more internet addiction, partly via stress — with interpersonal and academic stress carrying the strongest indirect links, and academic stress sitting at the center of the symptom network. The anomaly: within the punishment-related stress domain, higher self-control was associated with *higher* internet addiction.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the tidy assumption that self-control is uniformly protective, hinting that highly self-controlled teenagers under punitive pressure may use the internet as a compensatory escape — a hypothesis worth testing rather than a conclusion.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the reversal: the self-disciplined kid under heavy punishment at home or school looked *more* hooked online, not less. Open on the exam-pressure cooker of Chinese high school and the way academic stress sat at the hub of the whole network. Call corresponding author Wenjun Xu (Zhejiang Normal University), and an independent researcher on the Compensatory Internet Use Model.
studies.wider_angle: An education-outlet piece on what network analysis does to school mental health policy — if academic stress is the central node, then screen-time rules are treating the symptom while the exam system supplies the disease.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); self-reported throughout; Chinese high school students only, may not generalize; the non-linear punishment effect is a sub-analysis and could be a chance finding.

studies.title: A blood marker flags which methamphetamine users will still have thinking problems a year later
studies.ns_score_reason: a one-year prospective human cohort with a plausible biological marker; needs replication before it means anything clinically.
studies.the_study: Researchers in Taiwan measured plasma nectin-4, a cell adhesion molecule involved in synapse formation, in 126 patients with methamphetamine use disorder and 106 healthy controls, and tested executive function with the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test at baseline and again after a year of treatment. Patients had substantially higher nectin-4 levels, and higher baseline levels predicted more total and perseverative errors, fewer categories completed and lower conceptual scores a year later.
studies.why_it_matters: Executive function strongly shapes who stays in treatment, so a single blood draw that forecasts cognitive recovery would be genuinely useful — but this is one cohort and the mechanism linking a synaptic adhesion molecule to card sorting is unestablished.
studies.pitch_angle: Open with the clinical problem: two people start the same methamphetamine treatment program and a year later one can plan their week and the other can't. The surprise is that the difference may be readable in blood at the start. Call corresponding author Tzu-Yun Wang at National Cheng Kung University Hospital, and ask a neuroscientist outside the group what nectin-4 is actually doing at the synapse.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist medical or biotech outlet: the hunt for peripheral biomarkers in psychiatry, where almost nothing has made it to the clinic. Nectin-4 is already the target of an approved cancer antibody-drug conjugate — a story on molecules with double lives across oncology and psychiatry.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot establish causation); single center; no replication cohort; medication, abstinence and comorbidity effects on nectin-4 not resolved in the abstract; patients lost to follow-up unquantified here.

studies.title: Semaglutide blocks three different relapse triggers for fentanyl in rats
studies.ns_score_reason: the first test of the blockbuster weight-loss drug against opioid seeking, and it works on cue, drug and stress triggers; held back because it is rodents only.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Male Sprague-Dawley rats trained to self-administer fentanyl were given acute subcutaneous semaglutide at three doses, then exposed to the three classic relapse triggers: drug-associated cues, a priming infusion of fentanyl, and a pharmacological stressor (yohimbine). All doses fully prevented drug- and stress-induced reinstatement of fentanyl seeking; the two higher doses most effectively cut cue-induced seeking.
studies.why_it_matters: Anecdotal reports of GLP-1 drugs dampening cravings for alcohol, nicotine and opioids have run far ahead of the evidence; this is a controlled demonstration for fentanyl specifically, in the species where the relapse model was built — nothing more, but it strengthens the case for human trials.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the breadth: it isn't just that semaglutide reduced drug seeking, it shut down all three routes back to use, including stress. Open on the gap between the viral "Ozempic killed my cravings" posts and the near-absence of opioid data behind them. Patricia Sue Grigson at Penn State College of Medicine is the call — and note upfront that these are rats and that she consults for Eli Lilly.
studies.wider_angle: For a business or health-policy outlet: GLP-1 receptor agonists are being quietly repositioned as a general-purpose anti-craving class, from alcohol to gambling. Who is funding the human trials, what the regulators would need, and what happens to addiction medicine if a weekly injection outcompetes a treatment infrastructure built on daily dosing and clinic attendance.
studies.caveats: Animal study — findings may not translate to humans; male rats only; acute dosing, no chronic administration or tolerance data; senior author declares consultancy for Eli Lilly; no human craving or abstinence outcomes.

studies.title: Real-world reports flag unexpected psychiatric effects for the first pill approved for postpartum depression
studies.ns_score_reason: first large post-marketing safety sweep of zuranolone, with signals the label doesn't carry; disproportionality analyses cannot establish risk.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers mined the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System from Q3 2023 to Q2 2025 for reports naming zuranolone — the first oral drug approved for postpartum depression — as primary suspect, finding 648 patients and 299 preferred terms, analyzed with four standard signal-detection algorithms. Nervous system and psychiatric events dominated. Beyond labeled effects, intrusive thoughts and "feeling drunk" produced strong signals, alongside panic attack, suicidal ideation, dissociation, brain fog and speech disturbance, plus reports of exposure via breast milk.
studies.why_it_matters: Zuranolone is a neuroactive steroid acting on GABA-A receptors, the same family as benzodiazepines, and the signal pattern raises the question of whether the old GABAkine liabilities — sedation, dissociation, dependence potential — carry over into a drug given to new mothers.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on what zuranolone was sold as: a two-week course that lifts postpartum depression fast, a genuine advance. Then the awkward follow-up — what the first two years of real-world reports look like, including "feeling drunk" and breast milk exposure. Be explicit that spontaneous reporting systems show signals, not rates. Call the authors at Taizhou People's Hospital, and a pharmacovigilance methodologist plus a perinatal psychiatrist for balance.
studies.wider_angle: For a general-interest or women's health outlet: a feature on how little we know about any psychoactive drug in lactation, and why the breastfeeding mother remains one of medicine's least-studied patients despite a wave of new perinatal psychiatric drugs.
studies.caveats: Spontaneous reporting data — reporting bias, no denominator, cannot establish causation or incidence; confounding by indication (suicidal ideation is a feature of severe postpartum depression); no comparison arm; abstract does not report confounder adjustment.

studies.title: The immune system may be running the brain chemistry of addiction
studies.ns_score_reason: a coherent new framework with testable predictions for polysubstance use; it is a hypothesis paper built mostly on preclinical work.
studies.the_study: A review and hypothesis paper proposing that the glutamate disruption at the heart of addiction — specifically in the tripartite synapse of the nucleus accumbens — is orchestrated by neuroimmune signaling and the inflammasome, rather than merely accompanied by it. The authors argue this neuroimmune-glutamate circuit behaves as an opponent process whose direction depends on which drug is used and which phase of the addiction cycle someone is in, and they derive predictions for common polysubstance combinations.
studies.why_it_matters: If immune signaling gates the synaptic changes that drive relapse, then existing immunomodulatory drugs become candidate addiction treatments — and the drug-specific, phase-specific framing explains why anti-inflammatory approaches have given messy results so far.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is a reframe readers won't expect: addiction as partly an immune condition, and the reason anti-inflammatory drugs have failed inconsistently is that they were given at the wrong phase of the cycle. Open with the clinical oddity of someone whose withdrawal looks like being ill. Call lead author Cassandra D. Gipson at the University of Kentucky, and press her on which immunomodulators are closest to a human trial.
studies.wider_angle: A longer feature for a science magazine or specialist outlet on the neuroimmune turn across psychiatry — depression, schizophrenia, now addiction — and the pattern of early enthusiasm followed by underwhelming trials. What would count as the field finally getting it right?
studies.caveats: Review and hypothesis paper, not new data; evidence base is predominantly rodent; no human trial yet tests the central prediction; polysubstance predictions are untested.

studies.title: Psychedelics may work by loosening the scaffolding that holds brain circuits in place
studies.ns_score_reason: an elegant structural explanation for why one dose has effects lasting months; a review, and the human evidence is thin.
studies.the_study: This review synthesizes cellular and molecular evidence that classic psychedelics — psilocybin, LSD, DMT — do more than stimulate 5-HT2A receptors and the usual plasticity cascades (CaMKII, ERK, mTOR, BDNF). The authors make the case that the brain's extracellular matrix, and in particular the perineuronal nets that encase certain neurons and lock circuits into their adult configuration, is transiently loosened by psychedelics, reopening critical periods of plasticity that normally close in childhood.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers a physical answer to the puzzle of why a single dosing session can shift depression, PTSD or substance use for months — the drug may be briefly dissolving the structural cement that makes habits durable.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the image: psychedelics as a solvent for the mesh that keeps adult brains fixed. Open on the long-standing mystery of why psilocybin's benefits outlast the drug in the body by months. For addiction specifically, ask whether habit circuits need their nets loosened before new learning sticks — and what that implies about timing therapy to the window. Call corresponding author Xiaohui Wang (Changchun Institute of Applied Chemistry), plus an independent perineuronal net researcher.
studies.wider_angle: For a features desk: the critical-period reopening idea as a unifying theory of several very different interventions — psychedelics, ketamine, MDMA, even certain learning regimes — and the uncomfortable possibility that a brain with loosened nets is more suggestible as well as more plastic. That has real implications for how psychedelic therapy sessions are supervised.
studies.caveats: Review article, no new data; evidence predominantly from rodent work; the ECM mechanism has not been demonstrated directly in human brains; claims about addiction outcomes extrapolate from small clinical trials.

studies.title: Heavy digital media use is tied to higher BMI, and comfort eating sits in the middle of the link
studies.ns_score_reason: identifies a specific psychological route rather than another bare correlation, but cross-sectional and the mediated share is small.
studies.the_study: A cross-sectional survey of 610 Turkish young adults (mean age 21.6) measured digital addiction, motives for eating palatable food, body mass index and adherence to a Mediterranean lifestyle. Higher digital addiction scores were associated with higher BMI and lower Mediterranean lifestyle adherence, and palatable eating motives partially mediated both — though the indirect path accounted for only a small fraction of the total effect, and more so for BMI than for lifestyle.
studies.why_it_matters: It moves the screens-and-weight conversation past "sitting still" toward reward-driven eating motives — eating for pleasure, coping or social reasons — as one modest mechanism, which is a more tractable target than screen time itself.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is that the harm may not be the sitting, it's what the scrolling does to why you eat. Open on the specific scene of eating while watching, surrounded by food advertising engineered for exactly that moment. Be clear that the mediated effect is small and the design cannot show direction. Call corresponding author Rukiye Melisa Atan at Bandırma Onyedi Eylül University.
studies.wider_angle: For a food or public-health outlet: the erosion of the Mediterranean diet among young adults in Mediterranean-adjacent countries, and what replaces it when meals migrate from the table to the phone. A strong reported piece with regional data rather than a mechanism story.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational — cannot establish causation or mediation direction; self-reported BMI and behavior; single-country student-age sample, may not generalize; "digital addiction" is a contested construct.

studies.title: Gambling harm in Kazakhstan concentrates in middle-aged men, not the young
studies.ns_score_reason: useful corrective to the "young men on apps" stereotype in a rapidly liberalizing gambling market; the intervention arm is poorly specified.
studies.the_study: Two samples of Kazakh adults aged 18–65 — 782 assessed for gambling severity with the South Oaks Gambling Screen, and 148 enrolled in a rehabilitation program — were analyzed with regression alongside thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews. Men and 45- to 59-year-olds showed the highest severity; women and older participants the lowest. Low income and below-average education were both associated with greater dependency, and the authors report the rehabilitation program as highly effective.
studies.why_it_matters: Gambling expansion in Central Asia is outpacing research on it, and the age profile here cuts against the Western assumption that the at-risk group is young men with betting apps — but the effectiveness claim is reported without enough design detail to assess.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the demographic surprise: the people deepest in trouble were men in their fifties, not twenty-somethings, in a country where gambling has grown fast. Open on the social-protection angle — low income and low education compounding risk. Call Olga Tapalova at Abai Kazakh National Pedagogical University and press hard on what the rehabilitation program actually consisted of and whether it had a control group.
studies.wider_angle: For a global-affairs or investigative outlet: Central Asia as the gambling industry's next frontier, with regulation, casino-zone policy and online operators arriving faster than treatment services or research capacity.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional for the risk-factor component; self-reported screening instrument; rehabilitation effectiveness reported without described control condition or follow-up period in the abstract; single-country sample, may not generalize.

studies.title: When one man gambles online, the whole extended family pays the debt — and swears an oath
studies.ns_score_reason: vivid, genuinely novel cultural mechanisms in a setting where gambling is illegal; only nine interviewees, all gamblers.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Semi-structured interviews with nine married or formerly married men in Siirt, Türkiye, who currently or formerly gambled online were analyzed thematically. Four themes emerged: entry and the experience of addiction; disintegration of the nuclear family; household economic collapse and drift into crime; and stigma operating through kinship. Two mechanisms were distinctive to the setting — extended families collectively clearing a member's debts in exchange for religious oaths to stop, and stigma spreading through kin networks as a threat to collective family honor.
studies.why_it_matters: Almost all evidence on gambling's family harms comes from Western, individualist, legal-market settings; this shows the harm is routed through entirely different social machinery where gambling is illegal and kinship obligations are strong.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the oath — a family pooling money to clear a son's online betting debt, in exchange for a religious vow. It is a debt-relief and relapse-prevention system with no clinic in it, and it tells you something about where support actually comes from when the law offers none. Call Ahmet Bektaş at Gümüşhane University. Treat it as reporting on lived experience, not evidence of what works.
studies.wider_angle: For a long-form or international outlet: offshore betting sites in countries where gambling is banned — how the apps reach users, how money moves, and why prohibition tends to produce the harms without any of the harm-reduction infrastructure of regulated markets.
studies.caveats: Very small qualitative sample (N=9); all participants were gamblers, so family impacts are perceived rather than directly reported by affected relatives; single province; no quantitative outcomes; findings not generalizable.

studies.title: Gambling, gaming, social media and porn use may run through the same chain of thought
studies.ns_score_reason: a decent-sized test of a shared cognitive pathway across four behaviors, undercut by a design flaw the authors concede.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A community sample of 811 Iranian adults (43% male, mean age 27.7) completed self-report measures of early maladaptive schemas, desire thinking, craving and four problematic behaviors: gambling, gaming, social media use and pornography use. A serial model — schemas feeding desire thinking, which feeds craving, which feeds severity — fit acceptably, while a parallel model did not, and the serial indirect path held for all four behaviors. Critically, participants rated desire thinking and craving for a self-chosen activity that researchers did not record.
studies.why_it_matters: It supports the idea that deep-seated self-beliefs formed early fuel a specific mental habit — elaborating on anticipated pleasure — which then becomes craving across very different behaviors; but the unrecorded referent means the craving measures can't be matched to the behavior being predicted.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the shared engine: the same loop of rehearsing how good something will feel seems to sit behind gambling, gaming, scrolling and porn. Open on the moment before the behavior — the mental rehearsal, not the act. Call Mehdi Akbari at Kharazmi University, and Mark D. Griffiths at Nottingham Trent for the counterargument that lumping these together is premature. Disclose Griffiths's gambling industry funding and consultancy.
studies.wider_angle: For a psychology or health outlet: the diagnostic turf war over "behavioral addictions." Gambling disorder is in the manuals, gaming disorder partly so, social media and pornography are not — a piece on who decides, what evidence is required, and what happens to people seeking help for a condition that formally does not exist.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional — no temporal or causal ordering; all self-report; the target activity for desire thinking and craving measures was not recorded, limiting behavior-specific interpretation; single-country community sample, may not generalize; co-author Mark D. Griffiths reports research funding from Norsk Tipping and GambleAware and consultancy for gambling companies.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**

- **Self-control is not uniformly protective.** The new finding that highly self-controlled Chinese teenagers under punishment-related stress show *more* internet addiction ("Self-control protects teenagers from internet addiction — except when they are being punished", PMID 42727287) lines up with last month's backfire result that self-regulatory strategies tracked *higher* short-video addiction in low-inhibitory-control users ("Trying harder to self-regulate makes short-video addiction worse — for some people", PMID 42374874). Two independent samples, two different designs, same uncomfortable implication for screen-time advice.
- **Behavioral "addictions" are still being built out of cross-sectional self-report.** "Gambling, gaming, social media and porn use may run through the same chain of thought" (PMID 42801890) and "Heavy digital media use is tied to higher BMI, and comfort eating sits in the middle of the link" (PMID 42785564) repeat the pattern flagged last month in love addiction (PMID 42533520), AI addiction (PMID 42364395) and autistic traits/gaming (PMID 41742036) — contested constructs, assumed mediation direction, no temporal ordering.
- **Gambling research keeps moving out of the Western frame.** "Gambling harm in Kazakhstan concentrates in middle-aged men, not the young" (PMID 41887939) and "When one man gambles online, the whole extended family pays the debt — and swears an oath" (PMID 42704516) extend the geographic broadening seen last month in the Hong Kong card-pack audit (PMID 42611551) and the Spanish adolescent gambling-migration analysis (PMID 42599567).

**Counterpoints**

- **Emotion regulation demoted.** Last month, emotion-regulation difficulties were the explanatory engine in both "Exercise addiction and eating disorders look similar but come from different emotional places" (PMID 42504448) and "'Love addiction' is linked to distress and impulsivity — but only through a loss of emotional control" (PMID 42533520). This month's two-wave gambling study finds metacognitive beliefs outpredict emotion regulation ability, with the latter acting only as a buffer ("What gamblers believe about gambling predicts their trajectory better than how well they manage emotions", PMID 42143790).
- **The screens-cause-distress arrow gets weaker.** Previous entries treated internet use as an active ingredient — short-video use raising depressive symptoms via addiction in older adults (PMID 42374855), and reduced internet addiction predicting self-harm remission in boys (PMID 42633531). The new four-wave random-intercept analysis largely dissolves that within-person path ("Heavy phone use and depression travel together, but one may not be driving the other", PMID 42748880), and the authors concede the result flips with the model used.

**Advances**

- **Addiction neuroscience keeps leaving the reward circuit.** August gave dual-brain synchrony in abstinent heroin users (PMID 41941931) and a split of impulsivity into two near-non-overlapping connectomes (PMID 42562118); this month adds drug cues degrading basic somatosensory gating within milliseconds ("Seeing drug-related images breaks down basic sensory filtering in people who use methamphetamine", PMID 42740334). Three different tools, same message: the damage and the cue response are not confined to dopaminergic reward pathways.
- **Perinatal psychiatry thread continues.** "Women who smoke are twice as likely to develop postpartum depression" (PMID 42604887) is followed by the first large post-marketing sweep of zuranolone (PMID 42711976) — addiction-adjacent questions about GABAkine liability and breast milk exposure in the same patient group.

**New themes**

- **A treatment and biomarker pipeline appears.** The previous digest was almost entirely observational psychology and epidemiology. This batch brings semaglutide against three fentanyl relapse triggers (PMID 42228850), a plasma marker forecasting one-year executive function in methamphetamine use disorder (PMID 42379379), a neuroimmune-glutamate framework for relapse (PMID 42425280) and perineuronal net loosening as the durable mechanism behind psychedelics (PMID 41765343).
- **Methodology as the story.** The RI-CLPM deflation (PMID 42748880) and the network-analysis reframing of adolescent internet addiction (PMID 42727287) both make the analytic choice, rather than the finding, the newsworthy element.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Four studies in this batch point to addiction treatment being rebuilt out of materials borrowed from other fields — a weight-loss drug that shut down cue-, drug- and stress-induced fentanyl seeking in rats (PMID 42228850), a cell adhesion molecule already targeted by an approved cancer drug that forecasts cognitive recovery a year into methamphetamine treatment (PMID 42379379), an immunology-derived framework arguing that inflammasome signaling gates the glutamate changes behind relapse (PMID 42425280), and a structural account of psychedelics as transient solvents for the perineuronal nets that lock adult habits in place (PMID 41765343). Running alongside them is a cautionary case: the first two years of real-world reports on zuranolone, a first-in-class central nervous system drug, surfacing intrusive thoughts, "feeling drunk" and breast milk exposure that the label does not carry (PMID 42711976).

**Why pitch this now:** Anecdotal claims that GLP-1 drugs erase cravings for alcohol, nicotine and opioids have outrun the evidence by at least two years, and this is the moment when the actual preclinical and biomarker work is landing — along with a live example, in zuranolone, of what the first two years after approval look like when a novel psychoactive drug meets real patients.

**Angle:** A feature on addiction medicine's import trade: why the most promising candidate treatments for relapse were designed for obesity, cancer and inflammation, what it says about a field that has produced almost no new drugs of its own in decades, and what the post-marketing record of the last first-in-class psychiatric drug suggests about how the next wave will actually behave. For readers who have followed the GLP-1 story and want the pharmacology and the conflicts of interest rather than the testimonials.

**Potential headlines:**
- The next addiction drugs are coming from obesity clinics and cancer labs
- Addiction's most promising treatments were never designed for craving
- What happens to rehab if relapse can be treated with a weekly injection

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the mechanistic spread (GLP-1, neuroimmune gating, perineuronal nets) is exactly the Mind/Health territory, and the "repurposed drug" frame gives it narrative spine without overclaiming on rodent data.
- **STAT** — built for the pipeline-and-conflicts version: who is funding human GLP-1 trials in opioid use disorder, what regulators would need, and the Eli Lilly consultancy disclosed on the fentanyl paper.
- **Nature** (news feature) — would take the field-level argument that addiction pharmacology has been stalled and is now being revived by imports, with the nectin-4 oncology crossover as a concrete case.
- **Undark** — the sharpest home for the zuranolone counterweight: what post-marketing surveillance of a first-in-class psychiatric drug reveals, and why the breastfeeding patient remains almost unstudied.

### Study 1: Heavy phone use and depression travel together, but one may not be driving the other
**PMID:** 42748880 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Sample description overstates wave completion** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Chinese college students (N=851 retained) were surveyed four times across nine months, from September 2025 to June 2026"
- **Abstract says:** "Analyses retained 851 participants with at least two observed waves; 189 eligible students were first observed at T2."
- **Problem:** The study ran four waves, but the 851 analyzed participants were not all surveyed four times — inclusion required only two observed waves. The Caveats line notes the 189 T2 entrants, but the body text contradicts it by implying a complete four-wave sample.
- **Suggested fix:** "Chinese college students were surveyed across four waves from September 2025 to June 2026; 851 participants with at least two completed waves were retained for analysis."

**Issue B. NS fit score of 7 rests entirely on self-report** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — a rare four-wave, within-person test of the phone-causes-depression story that largely dissolves it; limited by self-report and a student sample."
- **Abstract says:** All measures are questionnaire-based; the authors' own conclusion is that the forward association "was model-dependent and did not establish a mechanism, causal effect, or statistically reliable directional difference."
- **Problem:** The design is genuinely strong for its class, but the entire evidence base is self-reported, single-country and single-population, and the headline finding is a model-dependent null. A 7 is at the top of what this can carry.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 6/10, with the same rationale text.

**Issue C. "Wider angle" overclaims the methodological reckoning** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "how the shift from cross-lagged to random-intercept models has quietly demolished a decade of 'X predicts Y' findings across psychology — screens, social media, loneliness, sleep"
- **Abstract says:** Reports only that in this sample the forward PSU→depression path was modest and model-dependent; makes no claim about the wider literature.
- **Problem:** "Demolished a decade of findings" is hype that outruns a single four-wave student study, and the digest's novelty tag "Overturns prior research" leans the same way. The angle is legitimate as a reported feature, but it should be flagged as a thesis to be tested with outside methodologists, not an established state of play.
- **Suggested fix:** "...how the shift from cross-lagged to random-intercept models has prompted re-examination of a decade of 'X predicts Y' findings across psychology — screens, social media, loneliness, sleep — and what, if anything, survives the reanalysis."

### Study 2: Seeing drug-related images breaks down basic sensory filtering in people who use methamphetamine
**PMID:** 42740334 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal attribution of GABAergic "damage" to stimulant use** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "what GABAergic damage from stimulants means for long-term cognition"
- **Abstract says:** "Adults who use methamphetamine exhibit altered gating responses and elevated spontaneous gamma activity in the somatosensory cortices, likely reflecting disruptions in GABAergic circuitry."
- **Problem:** The study is cross-sectional and group-comparative; it cannot establish that methamphetamine caused the inhibitory differences, nor that the differences constitute "damage." The digest's own Caveats say direction cannot be established, so the angle text contradicts the caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "...and what apparent GABAergic differences in people who use stimulants might mean for long-term cognition."

**Issue B. Timing claim not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a drug cue can degrade low-level sensory filtering within a fraction of a second"
- **Abstract says:** "Immediately before the first stimulation of each trial, participants viewed either a substance-related or neutral image."
- **Problem:** The abstract gives no cue-to-stimulus interval and reports no latency data, so the "fraction of a second" figure is unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "a drug cue presented immediately beforehand can degrade low-level sensory filtering"

**Issue C. "Breaks down" / "collapse" overstate the effect size** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Headline: "Seeing drug-related images breaks down basic sensory filtering"; pitch: "why its collapse implies drug cues hijack the brain far earlier in processing"
- **Abstract says:** "only those in the methamphetamine group exhibited weaker gating in the substance-cue compared to the neutral image condition"; "Substance-related cues accentuated gating deficits."
- **Problem:** The finding is a relative weakening of gating in one group, not a breakdown or collapse of the mechanism.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Drug-related images weaken basic sensory filtering in people who use methamphetamine"; pitch: "why this weakening implies..."

Note: the 7/10 score here is defensible — objective MEG measures, a within-subject experimental cue manipulation and a control group offset the modest N.

### Study 3: What gamblers believe about gambling predicts their trajectory better than how well they manage emotions
**PMID:** 42143790 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Treatment implication reverses the authors' own clinical recommendation** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "If beliefs about one's own thinking, rather than raw emotional coping, drive the escalation of gambling problems, treatment should target those beliefs directly — which is what metacognitive therapy does"
- **Abstract says:** "...a potential protective role of emotion regulation in the cycle. These findings highlight the important role of metacognitions in GD vulnerability and provide clinical insights such as incorporating emotion regulation training in Metacognitive Therapy based interventions for GD."
- **Problem:** The authors recommend *adding* emotion regulation training to metacognitive therapy, not substituting belief-targeting for emotional coping work. The digest's framing ("rather than raw emotional coping", NS fit note "demotes the fashionable emotion-regulation explanation") drops the protective finding and turns a two-wave observational result into a treatment prescription.
- **Suggested fix:** "Metacognitions were the stronger prospective predictor, but emotion regulation appeared to buffer the vicious cycle — which is why the authors suggest building emotion regulation training into metacognitive therapy for gambling disorder rather than choosing between them."

**Issue B. Example belief items not sourced from the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "beliefs such as 'gambling helps me control my thoughts' or 'my urge to gamble is uncontrollable'"
- **Abstract says:** Refers only to "positive and negative metacognitions about gambling"; no item wording is given.
- **Problem:** Plausible paraphrases of standard instrument items, but unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** Attribute to the measure explicitly, or soften: "beliefs about the usefulness of gambling thoughts and about the uncontrollability of gambling urges".

**Issue C. Disclosed conflict omitted from Caveats** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Caveats: ... funders include Chongqing municipal social science and education commission programs."
- **Abstract says:** "Given their role as Editor-in-Chief and an Associate Editor of Addictive Behaviors respectively, Prof. Marcantonio Spada and Prof. Anise M. S. Wu had no involvement in the peer review of this article..."
- **Problem:** Two of the study's authors hold senior editorial positions at the journal that published it. The digest proposes calling both as sources without noting this or that they are co-authors rather than independent commentators.
- **Suggested fix:** Add to Caveats: "Two authors (Spada, Wu) are the journal's Editor-in-Chief and an Associate Editor and were recused from peer review; both are study co-authors, not independent commentators."

### Study 4: Self-control protects teenagers from internet addiction — except when they are being punished
**PMID:** 42727287 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal language in headline and body for cross-sectional data** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** Headline: "Self-control protects teenagers from internet addiction"; body: "Lower self-control predicted more internet addiction, partly via stress"
- **Abstract says:** "self-control is significantly and negatively associated with IA, with negative life events partially mediating this relationship"; the paper frames everything as "association patterns."
- **Problem:** "Protects" and "predicted" assert causation and temporal order from a single-timepoint survey. The Caveats correctly say the design cannot establish causation, so the headline contradicts them.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Self-control is linked to less internet addiction in teenagers — except under punishment-related stress"; body: "Lower self-control was associated with more internet addiction, with stress partly accounting for the link."

**Issue B. "Symptom network" misnames the network** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "academic stress sitting at the center of the symptom network"
- **Abstract says:** "Network analysis further revealed that learning stress occupied a central position within the network structure."
- **Problem:** The network includes self-control components, stressor domains and internet addiction indicators, not symptoms alone.
- **Suggested fix:** "academic (learning) stress sitting at the centre of the overall network"

**Issue C. Nationality of sample inferred, not stated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "A survey of 4,305 Chinese high school students"
- **Abstract says:** "a large-scale survey of 4305 high school students" (author affiliations: Zhejiang Normal University, China)
- **Problem:** Reasonable inference from affiliation, but unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "A survey of 4,305 high school students, conducted by researchers at Zhejiang Normal University in China"

### Study 5: A blood marker flags which methamphetamine users will still have thinking problems a year later
**PMID:** 42379379 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline presents a group-level association as individual-level prediction** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "A blood marker flags which methamphetamine users will still have thinking problems a year later"
- **Abstract says:** "higher baseline nectin-4 levels were associated with greater total errors... after one year of treatment... Larger studies are needed to replicate the association between nectin-4 levels and executive function."
- **Problem:** The paper reports regression/GEE associations, not a validated predictive test — no cut-off, sensitivity, specificity or discrimination statistics are reported. "Flags which users will" implies a usable individual-level screen. The "Why it matters" paragraph hedges appropriately, but the headline does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "A blood marker is linked to how much thinking ability recovers a year into methamphetamine treatment"

**Issue B. Nectin-4 described with a function not given in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "plasma nectin-4, a cell adhesion molecule involved in synapse formation"
- **Abstract says:** "Nectin-4, a cell adhesion molecule linked to addiction severity"
- **Problem:** The synapse-formation role may be true in the wider literature but is unverifiable from abstract only; the abstract characterises it by its addiction-severity link.
- **Suggested fix:** "plasma nectin-4, a cell adhesion molecule previously linked to addiction severity"

### Study 6: Semaglutide blocks three different relapse triggers for fentanyl in rats
**PMID:** 42228850 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Blocks" overstates the cue-induced result** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Headline: "Semaglutide blocks three different relapse triggers for fentanyl in rats"
- **Abstract says:** "all doses of semaglutide fully prevented drug- and stress-induced reinstatement... while the mid (0.056 mg/kg) and higher doses (0.078 mg/kg) most effectively reduced cue-induced fentanyl seeking." Paper title: "attenuates cue-, drug-, and stress-induced fentanyl seeking."
- **Problem:** Cue-induced seeking was reduced, not blocked, and only at two of three doses. The body text gets this right; the headline flattens it.
- **Suggested fix:** "Semaglutide blunts all three classic relapse triggers for fentanyl in rats"

**Issue B. Novelty framing omits prior GLP-1 opioid findings** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 5/10 — the first test of the blockbuster weight-loss drug against opioid seeking, and it works on cue, drug and stress triggers"; "Anecdotal reports of GLP-1 drugs dampening cravings for alcohol, nicotine and opioids have run far ahead of the evidence"
- **Abstract says:** "a growing preclinical and clinical literature suggests that glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists may serve as new treatments for OUD. Exendin-4/exenatide and liraglutide have been found to reduce opioid intake, cravings, and cue-, drug-, and stress-induced opioid seeking."
- **Problem:** It is the first test of *semaglutide* specifically for opioid seeking, but other GLP-1 agonists have already shown the same three-trigger profile in opioids, and the abstract explicitly describes an existing preclinical and clinical literature — so "run far ahead of the evidence" and the framing of the triple effect as the novelty both need qualifying.
- **Suggested fix:** "...the first test of semaglutide specifically against opioid seeking, extending earlier results with exenatide and liraglutide to a once-weekly agent."

### Study 7: Real-world reports flag unexpected psychiatric effects for the first pill approved for postpartum depression
**PMID:** 42711976 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Author affiliation partly wrong** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call the authors at Taizhou People's Hospital"
- **Abstract says:** Hou W — "Department of Pharmacy, Wuxi Huishan District People's Hospital, Wuxi, Jiangsu, China"; Sun J and Lv X — The Affiliated Taizhou People's Hospital of Nanjing Medical University.

### Study 8: The immune system may be running the brain chemistry of addiction
**PMID:** 42425280 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Explanation for past anti-inflammatory trial failures asserted as finding** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the reason anti-inflammatory drugs have failed inconsistently is that they were given at the wrong phase of the cycle"; and in Why it matters, "the drug-specific, phase-specific framing explains why anti-inflammatory approaches have given messy results so far"
- **Abstract says:** "We outline a novel hypothesis that control of a newly defined neuroimmune-glutamate circuit and inflammasome is heavily dependent upon the type of addictive drug as well as on phase of the addiction cycle."
- **Problem:** The abstract offers this as an untested hypothesis and makes no claim about previous anti-inflammatory trials. Stating it as "the reason" presents a prediction as an established explanation.
- **Suggested fix:** "The authors' hypothesis implies that drug type and phase of the addiction cycle determine whether immunomodulation helps — a possible explanation, as yet untested, for inconsistent results from anti-inflammatory approaches."

The rest — tripartite synapse of the nucleus accumbens, inflammasome, opponent process, polysubstance predictions, Gipson at the University of Kentucky, and the review/hypothesis framing — is accurate.

### Study 10: Heavy digital media use is tied to higher BMI, and comfort eating sits in the middle of the link
**PMID:** 42785564 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Caveat asserts self-reported BMI, which the abstract does not state** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Caveats: ... self-reported BMI and behavior"
- **Abstract says:** "The data collection tools included Descriptive Information Form, Digital Addiction Scale (DAS), Palatable Eating Motives Scale (PEMS), BMI and MEDLIFE index."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not specify whether height and weight were measured or self-reported; a nutrition and dietetics department may well have measured them. Unverifiable from abstract only — asserting it as a limitation is as much a factual claim as asserting the opposite.
- **Suggested fix:** "self-reported questionnaire measures throughout; the abstract does not state whether BMI was measured or self-reported"

The statistics are otherwise handled well: both indirect effects were significant but small (β 0.048 for BMI, β −0.032 for MEDLIFE), and the digest correctly notes the mediation was more pronounced for BMI.

### Study 11: Gambling harm in Kazakhstan concentrates in middle-aged men, not the young
**PMID:** 41887939 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline contrast is with older, not younger, participants** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Gambling harm in Kazakhstan concentrates in middle-aged men, not the young"
- **Abstract says:** "Men and middle-aged individuals (45-59 years) were found to be most vulnerable to gambling addiction, while women and elderly participants showed lower levels of addiction."
- **Problem:** The explicit low-severity comparison group in the abstract is elderly participants; younger adults are not separately reported. The "not the young" contrast is an inference, and the abstract gives no figures for the 18–30 band.
- **Suggested fix:** "Gambling severity in Kazakhstan peaked among men aged 45 to 59 — not the demographic the stereotype predicts"

**Issue B. "Kazakh adults" conflates nationality with ethnicity** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Two samples of Kazakh adults aged 18–65"
- **Abstract says:** "The research included two samples of individuals aged 18 to 65" (study conducted in Kazakhstan; ethnicity not reported).
- **Problem:** "Kazakh" denotes an ethnic group; the abstract reports only that the study was carried out in Kazakhstan.
- **Suggested fix:** "Two samples of adults aged 18–65 in Kazakhstan"

The rehabilitation-effectiveness claim is correctly attributed to the authors and correctly flagged in Caveats as lacking design detail.

### Study 12: When one man gambles online, the whole extended family pays the debt — and swears an oath
**PMID:** 42704516 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline misattributes who swears the oath** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "When one man gambles online, the whole extended family pays the debt — and swears an oath"
- **Abstract says:** "Distinctive contextual mechanisms emerged, including the extended family's collective debt-clearing in exchange for religious oaths"
- **Problem:** The family clears the debt; the oath is given in exchange, by the gambling member. The headline reads as though the family swears it. The body text handles this correctly ("extended families collectively clearing a member's debts in exchange for religious oaths to stop").
- **Suggested fix:** "When one man gambles online, the extended family pays the debt — and he swears an oath"

The N=9, Siirt setting, four themes, perception-not-direct-experience limitation and non-generalisability are all accurately carried over, and the pitch correctly frames this as lived experience rather than evidence of effectiveness.

### Study 13: Gambling, gaming, social media and porn use may run through the same chain of thought
**PMID:** 42801890 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Shared engine" framing edges into a claim the authors explicitly disclaim** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The hook is the shared engine: the same loop of rehearsing how good something will feel seems to sit behind gambling, gaming, scrolling and porn."
- **Abstract says:** "The findings suggest possible cross-domain relevance of EMSs, desire thinking, and craving, but do not establish temporal or causal ordering, diagnostic equivalence, or a single underlying addiction process."
- **Problem:** The authors go out of their way to rule out the single-underlying-process reading; "the shared engine... sits behind" all four behaviours is exactly that reading. The digest's Caveats flag the cross-sectional design and the unrecorded referent, but not this explicit disclaimer, so the pitch angle's hook rests on a stronger result than the paper supports.
- **Suggested fix:** "The hook is a possible shared ingredient rather than a shared disorder: the loop of rehearsing how good something will feel shows up alongside all four behaviours — though the authors stress this does not establish a single underlying addiction process." Add the disclaimer to Caveats.

Sample details (811 Iranian adults, 43.4% male, mean age 27.70), the serial-versus-parallel model comparison, the unrecorded self-selected activity and the Griffiths funding and consultancy disclosures are all accurate.

**Cross-cutting note for the desk:** the recurring pattern is causal verbs ("protects", "predicted", "drive", "damage from") attached to cross-sectional or two-wave observational findings, while the Caveats boxes correctly disclaim causation. Harmonising headline and body verbs with the caveats would clear roughly half the flags above.
